title: Hidden Seed Oils: How to Actually Read a Food Label
seoTitle: How to Read Food Labels for Hidden Seed Oils
metaDesc: Seed oils turn up in a surprising number of supermarket foods. Here is where they hide and how to read a food label so your family can avoid them with ease.
author: Mr Wellness
intro: We are still surprised when we show someone the label on something they eat every day and they had no idea there was vegetable oil in it. It turns up in crackers, marinades, baby food, protein bars and plenty of other foods that sound completely fine. This quick guide is for anyone who wants to clean up their trolley without needing a university degree to do it.

sections.heading: The Names They Hide Behind
sections.content:
Seed oils such as canola, sunflower, safflower, soybean, cottonseed, corn and rice bran oil are in probably half the packaged food in your supermarket, yet they are rarely named clearly. Instead you will see terms like "vegetable oil", "vegetable fat" or "blended oil", which is basically a mix of the cheapest oils the manufacturer could source that week. In our house we call them the sneaky ones, because they hide in foods that sound wholesome.

These oils are high in omega-6 polyunsaturated fats, a type of fat that oxidises easily under heat. Think of butter left on a hot pan until it turns dark and acrid, except this happens inside a factory at extreme temperatures before the food even reaches the shelf.

sections.heading: The Simple Trolley Guide
sections.content:
Our honest default is to skip boxes and barcodes altogether and build meals from fruit, vegetables, meat, eggs and raw whole foods. Real life is not always that tidy, though, and we understand that, so here is the practical version. Pick up the packet and go straight to the ingredients list, not the nutrition panel. Scan it for canola, sunflower, safflower, soybean, corn, cottonseed, rice bran, or anything that simply says vegetable oil or vegetable fat.

If you see any of them in the first four or five ingredients, put the packet back. Manufacturers list ingredients by weight, so an oil near the top is there in a meaningful amount rather than a trace. A handful of genuinely good packaged options do exist, made with olive oil, coconut oil, butter or animal fats. They are worth tracking down once you know what to look for.

One thing to do today: take three packaged items from your pantry, turn them over and scan the ingredients for vegetable oil or any of the names above. There is no need for an overhaul, just a quick look and a bit more awareness of what is in there.

closing: Once you know the names to look for, reading a label takes only a few seconds, and the genuinely good options become much easier to spot.
pullQuote: They rarely call it seed oil on the label. They call it vegetable oil and hope you keep walking.
